items_missed: No booking attempt at all — the single largest miss. The customer said outright 'I'm trying to get this done today, so I can find a mover and get in here tomorrow' and Garrison had already confirmed 'we actually do have availability as early as tomorrow.' A ready-to-buy customer with a confirmed date and a delivered price was never asked to book. Nothing close to 'we have availability — want to go ahead and lock that in?' appears in the call.

No Worries Damage Coverage never named, and the $2,000 figure never stated — despite Garrison spending an entire paragraph telling the customer to go interrogate other movers about it: 'make sure you're asking about that, asking about their coverage, their insurance how they're gonna, you know, take care of you if something were to go wrong.' He set up the differentiator perfectly and then handed the answer to a competitor.

No deposit required never mentioned. This was a price-shopping customer explicitly comparing quotes ('you're literally $50 over what I thought was the highest price') — the zero-risk hold is the one lever that lets a shopper reserve tomorrow while still comparing, and it was never offered.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — notable because the customer needed the job done on a specific tight day ('get in here tomorrow'), which is exactly the anxiety that guarantee answers.

Effective insurance explanation missing entirely — no No Worries, no 60c/lb baseline, no valuation comparison, on a call whose whole emotional center was a brand-new closet system getting damaged in transit.

15-minute prorated increments after the minimum never explained. Garrison said 'all you have us for as long as you need us' and named the 2.5-hour minimum, but never told her what billing looks like past it.

No sense-check on the clock section. He closed the minimum explanation with 'So I did want to communicate that to you' rather than 'Does that make sense?' — and this was the exact moment the customer's price objection formed.
Never asked 'How are you today?' — went straight from 'this is garrison, how can I help you?' into the job.

Agenda statement given but with no timeframe and no confirmation. 'I'll gather some contact info and then some more move specific information like addresses and things like that' sets the sequence, but there is no '...takes about 10-15 minutes' and no 'Sound good?'
Moving stressor question never asked. He never asked what she was worried about — she surfaced her real concerns (price, same-week timing, protecting a new purchase) entirely on her own.

No time range given for the estimate, only a guess: 'I was thinking potentially an hour and a half depending.' The customer had already offered 'it should be no more than an hour' and he countered with a single point estimate rather than a bracketed range.
Stairs and walk distance were collected but never tied back to the estimate — 'five steps to the front' and the 30-40 foot walk were captured and then never explained as time variables.

No hours or specific way to reach the branch. The close was only 'if you have any questions feel free to let us know' — no number, no hours, no name to ask for.
Customer's name never used once. He collected 'Zen, vanloan V. as in victory, A-N space L-O-A-N' and then never said it again for the remaining seven minutes of the call.

Heavy verbal filler and false starts throughout — 'Let's see here, here. Well, yeah, okay. So that, I mean knowing that...', 'simply ply just regarding that photo address', and stacked 'absolutely, absolutely' / 'gotcha, gotcha, okay, cool' — which stretched a single-item quote to 11.4 minutes.

No alternative offered when the customer named the competitor category herself: 'I almost need to be like a two men and a truck sort of situation.' He agreed with the premise and offered nothing — no smaller-crew option, no different day tier, no referral.
top_strength: Garrison's discovery on an unfamiliar item was genuinely excellent, and his honesty at the price objection was the best moment on the call. He did not pretend to know what a closet system was — 'I admittedly am unfamiliar with what a closet system is. Would you mind explaining you're kind of describing what that is?' — and then worked it into a load-plannable picture: assembly status, that it was 'five direct boxes' plus loose fronting pieces, building type at both ends, five steps at origin, 'one storing, no steps at all' at destination, and a walk distance he asked for specifically ('if you had to estimate how far of a walk, would you say it is kind of overall from where we would be able to park our truck'). He led with availability before anything else and said so out loud: 'that's of course the first thing I did want to cover just to ensure you know, we did have the date you were looking for.' His trip-fee handling under pushback was calm and correct — when she argued her address wasn't really Hutto he held the line without friction: 'it not unfortunately doesn't change regarding the trip fee because it's actually calculating based on physical location... No, I do appreciate the clarification.' And when the math went against him he told the truth instead of squirming: 'I definitely understand that we might not be the best financial option in this particular case. Knowing that minimum' and 'we are admittedly a little bit better when it comes to larger scale moves with the smaller things. You know, it's not necessarily always the cheapest.' That honesty is what earned the call's closing line — 'You gave me a lot to think about. Thank you.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Garrison built the case for No Worries Damage Coverage and then never delivered it. He told this customer to go shop other movers on exactly our strongest differentiator — 'if your mover ends up breaking it, damaging it, scuff it, scratching it... make sure you're asking about that, asking about their coverage' — without ever stating ours. The line he needed, right there, was: 'And here's ours, Zen — No Worries Damage Coverage, up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse any accidental damage, included in that hourly rate at no extra cost. Most movers will only cover 60 cents a pound, which on a brand-new nine-foot closet system means they hand you about twenty dollars for a cabinet you just paid hundreds for. That's the gap I'd want you comparing.' That single paragraph reframes $595 from 'fifty dollars over my highest quote' into insurance on a new purchase, and it is the only argument on this call that could have beaten the price objection. Second priority, and it is nearly as costly: there was no booking attempt. She said 'I'm trying to get this done today, so I can find a mover and get in here tomorrow' and he had already confirmed tomorrow was open — that is a buying signal plus a confirmed date, and the call still ended on 'I'll shoot that email over to you.' Pair the coverage pitch with the no-deposit close: 'There's no deposit and nothing due today, so let me hold tomorrow morning for you while you finish comparing — if you find something better, you cancel and it costs you nothing.' A price shopper who has to choose today will almost always take a free hold. Third, the clock section is where the objection was actually born, and he narrated the minimum without a sense-check. Say the 2.5-hour minimum, then the 15-minute prorated increments after it, then 'Does that make sense?' and let her react before you name the total. Business risk to fix in EMMA today: the contact data on this lead is not trustworthy, and the entire follow-up plan rests on it. The email came through two different ways in one breath — 'Zen. Lo @yahoo.com Z-E-N-L-O-P-E-R @yahoo.com' — and he never read it back. The callback-number confirmation came back as 'this is Marshall,' which was never resolved. He also never captured the origin zip on 2120 Denton Drive. Verify the address, the number, and the zip before that comparison email goes out, because if it bounces this lead is simply gone.
